title: Year two opens: back in the cycle
hook: last year stopped at Va'era; this year the Torah is read through to its last word

segments.voice: Yesterday we stood at the big lookout and blessed the arriving. Your line was you kept me alive for this. Did one first thing of the day get that line? Now the path turns into year two. Day three hundred thirty-two.

A Torah scroll is two wooden rollers with a long ribbon of parchment wound between them, and fully unrolled it would run longer than a city bus. On Shabbat morning someone opens it on the reading table, and it's already sitting where last week's reading stopped. Nobody rewinds to the start because they missed a week. Nobody skips ahead to the good part. The scroll simply waits at the place it was left. Last year our reading stopped in the middle of Exodus, in a portion called Va'era, with hail and fire falling on Egypt together. Year two picks up from exactly there.
screen: `TWO ROLLERS, ONE LONG RIBBON.` → `IT WAITS WHERE YOU LEFT IT.` → `WE STOPPED AT VA'ERA.`

segments.voice: The Torah, the five books of Moses, is divided into fifty-four weekly portions. Each one is called a parashah, which simply means a section; plenty of people say parsha. Each portion is named for an early, distinctive word in it. Bereshit, in the beginning. Va'era, and I appeared. Next comes Bo, which means come. Across the Jewish year the portions are read one after another, and in weeks when the calendar runs short, two are read together so the whole thing fits. The annual cycle grew up among the Jews of Babylonia. The Talmud remembers that Jews in the Land of Israel took about three years to finish, and today some congregations read a third of each portion, a three-year rhythm with ancient roots. Either way, the end is not an end. On the holiday of Simchat Torah, the last lines of Deuteronomy are read, and straight after them, the first lines of Genesis. People dance with the scrolls in their arms. The circle closes and opens in the same morning. The sayings of the fathers keep a line from a sage called Ben Bag Bag about the Torah: turn it and turn it, for everything is in it. A year-two reader turns it again. Here's the plan. First, the rest of Exodus, Bo to the finished tabernacle. Then Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy, to the very last word. Then the siddur, the prayer book, page by page. Then the Jewish year, in depth.
screen: `FIFTY-FOUR PORTIONS: PARASHAH.` · `NAMED FOR AN EARLY WORD.` · `ONE YEAR, OR THREE.` · `SIMCHAT TORAH: THE END MEETS THE START.` · then, large: `TURN IT AND TURN IT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find your place in the cycle. Settle, and breathe. Picture the scroll lying open at the spot where you left it, waiting, not annoyed that you were gone. Think of one thing in your own life you set down and meant to pick up again: a book, a habit, a conversation. Don't scold yourself. Just notice where your marker is. After the bell, if you like, look up which portion synagogues read this coming Shabbat. Any Jewish calendar lists it. The bell holds the time.
Year two opens. We pick up the Torah where we left it, at Bo, and read through to the last word, then open the prayer book.
Your line: the scroll keeps rolling. Today, pick up one thing you set down, right where you left it, without starting over. Day three hundred thirty-two.

howItsDone: Synagogues read one Torah portion each Shabbat, in order, across the year; on Simchat Torah the last lines of Deuteronomy are read and the first lines of Genesis follow at once. Many Jews study the week's portion at home as well.

original.note: Hebrew: a section; the weekly Torah portion. many say parsha.

trapdoor: what you thought: you read the Torah once and you're done.
what it means: it's read every year in a cycle, and picking up where you stopped is the practice.
what a scholar hears: Talmud Megillah 29b recalls Jews in the Land of Israel finishing the Torah in about three years.

sources.ref: Simchat Torah reading: Deuteronomy 33–34 and Genesis 1

notes: Fifty-four portions is the standard count; in many years some are combined. Confirm phrasing.

Triennial cycle: Megillah 29b mentions 'the people of the West' (Land of Israel) completing the Torah in three years. The modern triennial reading in some Conservative and Reform congregations is a different arrangement; described loosely as a three-year rhythm with ancient roots. Check.
Ben Bag Bag's saying is Avot 5:22 in common numbering (5:25/5:26 in some); paraphrased.
'Longer than a city bus' for a fully unrolled scroll: Torah scrolls vary, commonly tens of meters; verify the image is safe.
The path's order (rest of Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy, then siddur, then the Jewish year) follows the y2.md header; the teach states it as the plan.
